Now let me compile the verse-by-verse commentary notes from all the sources I've gathered.

---

# Job 38:21–41 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 21: "Surely you know, for you were already born! And the number of your days is great!"

- **Traditional reading (irony):** This is the climax of God's irony that has underlain the whole address. The sense is: "Doubtless you know all this, since you were born at creation and your days are so many!" Job was, in reality, "of yesterday" and knew nothing. The sarcasm is biting but purposeful — to humble Job. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Pulpit Commentary: biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-21.htm)
- **Gill (Baptist):** Job did not know when he was born, nor of whom, except by the report of others; how much less could he know what happened before his birth? God, by contrast, knows all these things beforehand. Also notes the Targum's rendering: "Didst thou know then that thou shouldest be born, and the number of thy days many?" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-38.html)
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** "Perhaps Job was so old and so wise that he did indeed know these things. If this were the case, God invited Job to speak up at any time." The tone is playful yet humbling. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Biblehub summary:** God probes Job's knowledge with gentle irony: Job was not yet born when light and darkness were established. (biblehub.com/job/38.htm)

---

## v. 22: "Have you entered the storehouses of snow or observed the storehouses of hail…"

- **Traditional reading:** Snow and hail are pictured as stored in divine "treasuries" or "storehouses," from which God draws them forth. Snow is vapour congealed in the air before forming drops; hail is rain falling through cold, dry air. The question is whether Job has toured these celestial warehouses. (JFB: ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb.x.xviii.xxxix.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Biblehub summary:** Snow and hail are pictured as weapons stored for times of trouble and war, hinting at future judgments. (biblehub.com/job/38.htm)

---

## v. 23: "…which I hold in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of war and battle?"

- **Traditional reading:** God has reserved hail and snow as instruments of judgment. Biblical examples include the hail against Egypt (Exodus 9:24), against the Canaanites at Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11), against apostate Israel (Isaiah 28:2), against Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38:22), and in the Great Tribulation (Revelation 16:20–21). (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Kretzmann (Lutheran):** Snow and hail are reserved for "seasons of distress upon mankind, against the day of battle and war." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/job-38.html)

---

## v. 24: "In which direction is the lightning dispersed, or the east wind scattered over the earth?"

- **Traditional reading:** The question concerns the path or "way" by which light (lightning) is distributed to all the inhabitants of the earth. The east wind, a fierce desert wind, is also beyond man's calculation. Both phenomena defy human prediction in their swiftness and changes. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Kretzmann: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/job-38.html)
- **JFB:** Light travels from the sun to the earth, some ninety million miles, in about eight minutes — man cannot trace its path. (ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb.x.xviii.xxxix.html)

---

## v. 25: "Who cuts a channel for the flood or clears a path for the thunderbolt…"

- **Traditional reading:** Literally, "Who has cleft a channel for the water-flood." God engineers the drainage systems of the earth — the wadis and riverbeds that carry torrential rains — and directs the path of the thunderbolt. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Biblehub summary:** God describes carving channels for storms, fathering rain, and forming ice and frost — all without human aid. (biblehub.com/job/38.htm)

---

## v. 26–27: "…to bring rain on a barren land, on a desert where no man lives, to satisfy the parched wasteland…"

- **Traditional reading:** God causes rain to fall even on uninhabited wilderness, proving that man does not guide its course. Such rain is not wasted — God has wise design in it. God is mindful of His creation independently of the needs of man. The rain "satisfies" the desolate waste, causing tender grass to sprout. (JFB: ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb.x.xviii.xxxix.html; Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html)
- **Enduring Word:** These verses continue the theme that God alone manages the hydrological systems of the earth. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)

---

## v. 28: "Does the rain have a father? Who has begotten the drops of dew?"

- **Traditional reading:** Using the metaphor of parenthood, God asks Job who fathered the rain and begot the dew. In the ancient Near East, pagan myths spoke of rain and other natural phenomena being produced by gods. The Lord dismisses such ideas and claims sole creative responsibility. (Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist, quoted in Enduring Word):** Likened rain to the grace of God: "If both Houses of Parliament were to be called together … and they were unanimously to pass an act ordering the rain to fall, he that sitteth in the heavens would laugh … the key of the rain is in no hand but that of Jehovah. It is exactly so with the grace of God." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)

---

## v. 29–30: "From whose womb does the ice emerge? Who gives birth to the frost from heaven, when the waters become hard as stone and the surface of the deep is frozen?"

- **Traditional reading:** Continuing the birth/parenthood metaphor, God claims to be the one who brings forth ice and frost. The imagery of "womb" (v. 29) and "giving birth" personifies these phenomena. Water loses its familiar liquid quality and "hides itself" by becoming like stone — a poetic description of freezing. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Ellicott:** "The waters hide themselves and become like stone. Water loses its familiar quality, and is turned into stone." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html)

---

## v. 31: "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loosen the belt of Orion?"

- **Traditional reading (two main interpretations of "chains"):**
  1. **"Sweet influences":** The Hebrew word (maʿăḏannôt) can mean "pleasures" or "delights" (from the root meaning "to be soft, pliant"), hence the KJV's "sweet influences." The Pleiades appear in spring and seem to usher in the pleasant season. God asks if Job can regulate these seasonal influences. (biblehub.com/job/38-31.htm; Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html)
  2. **"Chains/bands":** Most modern critics prefer "chains" or "fastenings" — the invisible gravitational links that bind star clusters together. Can Job draw the stars closer or loosen them? (Pulpit Commentary: biblehub.com/job/38-31.htm)
- **Orion's belt:** The three bright belt stars form a familiar pattern. God asks if Job can "loosen" Orion's bands — that is, alter the forces that hold the constellation in its ordered course. The pairing of "binding" and "loosening" shows God's complete mastery over cosmic stability. (biblehub.com/job/38-31.htm)
- **Gill (Baptist):** The Pleiades rising in spring bring "pleasantnesses of the season" which cannot be restrained. Orion appears in winter, bringing stormy winds, rain, snow, and frost. Spiritually, this teaches Job he cannot turn "the winter of adversity into the spring of prosperity" — he must submit to God's sovereignty. (studylight.org/bible/job/38-31.html, Gill's notes)
- **Grant's Commentary (Brethren):** Notes that astronomers later discovered "the whole solar system is moving forward around Alcyone, the brightest star in the Pleiades" — such are the "chains" that captivate the solar system. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-38.html)

---

## v. 32: "Can you bring forth the constellations in their seasons or lead out the Bear and her cubs?"

- **Traditional reading:** "Mazzaroth" is commonly understood as the signs of the Zodiac or the constellations in their seasons. The "Bear" (or "Great Bear") with her "cubs" probably refers to Ursa Major (the three stars in the tail being the "cubs"). God alone brings them out in their proper times. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Biblehub** notes a footnote: "Or bring forth Mazzaroth in its season" and "Or Leo or Arcturus" for the Bear. (biblehub.com/job/38.htm)

---

## v. 33: "Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you set their dominion over the earth?"

- **Traditional reading:** The "ordinances" or "laws of the heavens" refer to the recurring seasons and the heavenly bodies' power to influence the earth. Job could observe these patterns but could not explain the natural forces governing them, let alone set their dominion. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics:** "We cannot affect the heavenly bodies. They roll on their age-long courses in sublime indifference to our greatest achievements … This is a lesson in humility. Yet have we not a grand encouragement in knowing that the Lord of the starry universe is our Father who cares for us?" (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/38.htm)
- **Peake's Commentary (modern scholarship):** Suggests a different pointing yields "Dost thou make the heavens to know the laws" — i.e., do you lay down the laws for them? (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-38.html)

---

## v. 34: "Can you command the clouds so that a flood of water covers you?"

- **Traditional reading:** Job is powerless over the clouds. He cannot lift his voice to them and command an abundance of water. God moves from the distant constellations down to the nearer phenomena of clouds and lightning. (Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Peake's Commentary:** Reads with LXX, "that abundance of waters may answer thee" — personifying the clouds as obedient servants. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-38.html)

---

## v. 35: "Can you send the lightning bolts on their way? Do they report to you, 'Here we are'?"

- **Traditional reading:** The lightning bolts are personified as messengers who obey God instantly, reporting "Here we are!" like servants awaiting orders. Job cannot command such obedience from the elements. (Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Ellicott:** This section belongs with the personification of lightning (see note on v. 36) — God may be attributing intelligence to the lightning itself as His minister. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html)

---

## v. 36: "Who has put wisdom in the heart or given understanding to the mind?"

- **This verse is notably disputed among commentators:**

  **Interpretation A — Human wisdom (traditional KJV/AV view):**
  God asks who gave man intelligence and understanding. Job's intellectual capacity was not the product of random chance but was designed by a great Designer. The connection is: "Look at these wonders; who endowed your mind so that you can even contemplate them?" God appeals to the fact that He endowed man with intelligence as a proof of His greatness. (Barnes, in biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-36.htm; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)

  **Interpretation B — Celestial phenomena (many modern scholars):**
  The Hebrew words rendered "inward parts" (ṭuḥôt) and "heart" (śekvî) are of uncertain meaning. Since a reference to the human mind interrupts a section on celestial phenomena, many argue the words refer to meteorological phenomena — possibly "dark clouds" and "meteor," or "thunderbolts" and "tempest." The sense would be: "Who has put wisdom in the thunderbolts? Who has given understanding to the storm?" — meaning that these phenomena seem to act with intelligent purpose as God's ministers. (Schultens, Rosenmüller, Umbreit; Revised Version margin; biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-36.htm; studylight.org/commentary/job/38-36.html)
  
  **Pulpit Commentary:** "There is great difficulty in supposing a sudden transition from clouds and lightning … to the human understanding … with a return to clouds and rain in ver. 37." Therefore many "best critics" refer it to the intelligence that may be regarded as existing in the clouds themselves. (biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-36.htm)

  **Keil & Delitzsch:** Maintain the traditional psychological interpretation — God put wisdom in the inward parts of man. (mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/job/38.htm)

  **Biblehub footnote (BSB):** Notes an alternative translation: "Who has given the ibis wisdom, that is, wisdom about the flooding of the Nile" — reflecting the Egyptian context. (biblehub.com/job/38.htm)

---

## v. 37: "Who has the wisdom to count the clouds? Or who can tilt the water jars of the heavens…"

- **Traditional reading:** "The bottles (water jars) of heaven" are the clouds, conceived as skins full of water. "Tilting" them means pouring out their liquid contents as rain. Only God can number the clouds or pour them out. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Peake's: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-38.html)
- **Kretzmann (Lutheran):** "Who can number the clouds in wisdom, appointing to them their number and extent? Or who can stay the bottles of heaven, who tilts them, who pours out their liquid contents?" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/job-38.html)
- **Ellicott** notes the verb can be understood in two opposite senses: pouring out the bottles or laying them up in store. Context determines which. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html)

---

## v. 38: "…when the dust hardens into a mass and the clods of earth stick together?"

- **Traditional reading:** After rain, the dust that was loose becomes a firm mass; the clods cake together into hardness. God controls this process. (Kretzmann: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/job-38.html)
- **JFB (alternative rendering):** "Rather, pour itself into a mass by the rain, like molten metal; then translate v. 38, 'Who is it that empties,' etc., 'when,' etc.?" The English Version is also tenable: the dust is "caked into a mass" by heat, like molten metal, before the rain falls. (ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb.x.xviii.xxxix.html)
- **Enduring Word:** "When the dust hardens in clumps, and the clods cling together" — God alone orchestrates the cycle from dry dust to rain-soaked soil. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)

---

## v. 39: "Can you hunt the prey for a lioness or satisfy the hunger of young lions…"

- **Traditional reading:** God now moves from the inanimate creation to the animal kingdom. Job cannot provide food for the lioness or satisfy the appetite of young lions. This opens a new section (some say a new chapter should begin here) surveying the animal creation. (Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html; Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** "Verse 39 inquires of Job whether or not he will hunt or stalk the prey (food) for the lion, to satisfy his hunger? … Or is he able or willing to fill the recurring, voracious appetite of the young, growing lions?" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-38.html)
- **Grant's Commentary:** "God is not only infinitely great, but He has a heart of kindness and care for all His creation. In this section He begins with the beasts of prey, with which we should not likely begin, for we think of them as needing no outside care for they are predators. But they require the care of God as do all other creatures." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-38.html)

---

## v. 40: "…when they crouch in their dens and lie in wait in the thicket?"

- **Traditional reading:** Describes lions crouching in their dens or lurking in covert places, waiting for prey. The verse completes the picture begun in v. 39. God cares for even these fierce predators in their hidden lairs. (Gill: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-38.html; Garner-Howes: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-38.html)
- **Gill (Baptist):** Notes some understand this of old lions who, for want of strength, lie couchant waiting for any prey that passes. The same places are used by younger lions too. Both are "emblems of wicked men, cruel persecutors, and bloodthirsty tyrants." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-38.html)

---

## v. 41: "Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food?"

- **Traditional reading:** God provides for the raven — a creature considered mean, voracious, and of ill omen. Jesus later uses this same example: "Consider the ravens: They do not sow or reap … yet God feeds them" (Luke 12:24). The young ravens' cry is interpreted by God as a cry to Him. If God cares for ravens, how much more for humans. (Gill: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-38.html; Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-38.html)
- **Enduring Word:** "God provides food for the birds (Matthew 6:26); it would be impossible for Job or any other man to do so. God here is reminding Job of the distance between Himself and Job." Also quotes Smick: "The choice is somewhat random, as if Yahweh is saying, 'Here are only a few specimens of all my creatures … all are under my care and dominion.'" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/)
- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics:** "Job is asked to think of the raven, and consider how it is provided for. Christ answers the same thought when He points to the ravens as an encouragement to faith." (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/38.htm)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** "God asks Job if he is able to order nature by providing wild animals with food … while protecting timid animals when they give birth and care for their young." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/job-38.html)
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** "The Lord switches, from the care of the noble lion, to the croaking raven, considered to be of ill-omen; Yet God cares for it. Will Job acknowledge it, with penitent humility? … When the young wander, cry, croak for food, God provides for, cares for them. How much more for men! Luke 12:24; Philippians 4:19." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-38.html)

---

## Summary: Where Protestant traditions differ

| Topic | Reformed/Presbyterian | Baptist | Pentecostal/Charismatic | Lutheran |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Overall thrust** | God's sovereignty in creation silences human presumption (JFB, ccel.org) | Gill emphasizes God's particular providence and the spiritual application (studylight.org/geb) | Enduring Word stresses God's personal presence — the comfort is that God *showed up*, not that He explained (enduringword.com) | Kretzmann emphasizes God's supremacy over all forces and man's insignificance (studylight.org/kpc) |
| **v. 31 (Pleiades/Orion)** | JFB: sweet influences refer to seasonal effects | Gill: spiritualised — winter of adversity vs. spring of prosperity; submit to sovereignty | Enduring Word: playful tone of God exposing man's powerlessness | Not distinctly covered |
| **v. 36 (wisdom in heart)** | Keil & Delitzsch: traditional psychological reading | Gill not available for this verse in gathered data | Enduring Word: human intelligence given by Intelligent Designer | Not distinctly covered |
| **v. 39-41 (animals)** | JFB: God gives instinct to hunt prey | Gill: lions as emblems of wicked men; Garner-Howes: God's care for even "ill-omened" raven | Enduring Word: God's intimate governance over wild creatures | Kretzmann: God's providential care placing Him far above all creatures |

---

## Other Views

- **Modern scholarship (v. 36):** Peake's Commentary and the Revised Version margin argue the obscure Hebrew terms refer to physical phenomena (dark clouds, meteor), not human inward parts. The BSB footnote offers "Who has given the ibis wisdom" — a possible reference to the Egyptian ibis and Nile flooding. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-38.html; biblehub.com/job/38.htm)

- **Catholic / Orthodox:** No results were returned from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for these specific verses within the search constraints. These sites would generally affirm the traditional reading, often drawing on patristic sources (e.g., Gregory the Great's *Moralia in Job*). This could not be confirmed from the available page fetches.

- **NET Bible notes (netbible.org):** No results were returned within search constraints for specific NET notes on this passage.
